# Browser Selection and Diagnostics

Yantra gives you one honest, local answer to _"which browser will Yantra actually use, and will it
work?"_ — and one way to change that answer. You can persist a choice, override it for a single
command, list what the machine has, and test the selected browser against the primitives Yantra
actually needs.

Every command in this area is local. None of them contacts a version server, downloads anything, or
looks for a newer browser.

## What It Does

### Persists which browser Yantra launches

`yantra browser use <auto|managed|system>` writes the choice into `config.yaml` as installation
state, so every later command — `run`, `resume`, `ask`, `research`, `do`, and the recorder — resolves
the same binary.

- `auto` prefers a ready Yantra-managed installation and otherwise falls back to external Chrome or
  Chromium discovery.
- `managed` requires an existing ready managed installation. Without one the command fails and names
  `yantra browser install`; an unusable managed record fails with the recorded reason rather than
  quietly running some other browser.
- `system` uses external discovery only. Adding `--path <absolute-executable>` selects one specific
  external binary instead.

Both fields are written together. `auto` and `managed` always clear a previously configured path, so
the file never holds a stale executable path under a source that cannot mean one.

### Validates a path without starting a browser

`browser use system --path P` checks that `P` is absolute, exists, is a regular file (or a symlink to
one), is readable, and — on macOS and Linux — is executable. Each failure has its own message: a
missing file, a directory, a relative path, a dangling symlink, and a file without execute permission
do not read alike.

Compatibility is deliberately **not** probed here. Setting a preference never costs a browser launch,
and it does not fail on a host where launching is the broken thing. After committing, the command
reports the compatibility Yantra already knows about — `tested`, `capability-checked`, or
`unverified` — and when it is `unverified` it prints the exact `yantra browser check` command to run.

A custom path that lands inside the Yantra-managed browser root is treated as managed-owned even
though it arrived through `system`. It must be the exact ready managed executable; a path into a
superseded installation, or one that crosses into the managed root through a symlink or junction, is
refused.

### Overrides one invocation without writing configuration

`--browser <auto|managed|system>` and `--browser-path <absolute-executable>` select a browser for a
single command and change nothing on disk.

- `--browser-path` alone implies `system`.
- `--browser system` with no path **clears** a configured custom path for that invocation, because
  the override is a whole selection rather than a field-by-field merge.
- Pairing `--browser-path` with `auto` or `managed` is a conflict, and a relative path is rejected.

Precedence is invocation flags, then the `config.yaml` selection, then `auto`.

These flags are registered only on the commands that can actually launch a browser: `run`, `resume`,
`ask`, `research`, `do`, and `browser check`. Everywhere else — including `daemon`, `schedule`,
`init`, `list`, `config`, `doctor`, `browser list`, and `browser use` — they are rejected as unknown
options, because a flag a command cannot honor is a dead control rather than shared vocabulary.

### Lists what the machine has

`yantra browser list` reports the current selection and whether it came from `config.yaml` or the
default, the effective installation with its ownership, path, version and channel, the managed
installation or `absent`, the external browsers discovery found, the orphan count with reclaimable
bytes, and the driver version with its tested pairing. Exactly one listed browser is marked
effective, and a browser found by both managed state and external discovery is listed once.

`list` is an inventory, so a broken selection is rendered as data with its remediation and the
command still exits `0`. Failing is the job of a launching command and of `browser check`.

### Tests the selected browser locally

`yantra browser check` runs a fresh isolated probe — its own headless session with its own ephemeral
profile, closed on success and on failure — for both capability sets Yantra uses: `automation` and
`recorder`. A cached success never short-circuits it.

The report names the driver version, the tested pairing, the probe revision, the actual browser
version, path, ownership, and how the selection was made, then one row per required capability with
the reason that capability is required. On failure it renders the failure class and its own
remediation:

- `missing-runtime-libraries` names the operating-system packages the downloaded Chrome build needs,
  read from the installation's own dependency list;
- `capability-failure` names exactly the primitives that failed, without implying a version mismatch
  caused it, and marks rows that never ran with the prerequisite that failed;
- `launch-environment` keeps the supported-browser guidance.

A browser newer than the driver's tested pairing is **normal operation**, reported as
`capability-checked` rather than as a warning: Chrome ships Stable faster than this repository bumps
its driver, so being ahead of the pairing is the usual state.

### Reports provenance from `doctor`

`yantra doctor` reports three browser checks, all read from the same local inventory `browser list`
renders, so the two cannot disagree:

- `browser.selection` — configured source and origin, ownership, canonical executable, actual
  version, or the resolution error with its remediation and the alternatives found;
- `browser.compatibility` — the last known local evidence, reported honestly as `unverified` when
  nothing has been checked and `stale` when the evidence describes a different binary, never
  manufactured by launching something;
- `browser.managed` — the managed root, the ready build or `absent`, and the orphan count with
  reclaimable bytes.

Doctor launches no browser, installs nothing, and collects no orphans. Its one-hour report cache is
keyed on the effective browser identity, so changing the selection produces fresh output without
`--refresh`.

## How to Use It

Select a browser and confirm what will run:

```bash
yantra browser list
yantra browser use auto
yantra browser use managed
yantra browser use system
yantra browser use system --path /opt/google/chrome/chrome
```

Test the selected browser, or a specific binary, before trusting it:

```bash
yantra browser check
yantra browser check --browser-path /opt/google/chrome/chrome
yantra browser check --json
```

Override one command without changing the saved choice:

```bash
yantra run monthly-invoices --browser system
yantra ask "what changed in the spec" --browser-path /opt/chromium/chrome
```

Read the persisted binding through the ordinary configuration surface:

```bash
yantra config get browser.source
yantra config get browser.executable_path
yantra doctor --json
```

## Inputs and Outputs

Terminal output states the committed source, the resolved path, and ownership. With `--json` each
command emits exactly one envelope on stdout carrying the current protocol `schemaVersion` and a
`kind`:

| Command         | `kind`          | Payload                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| --------------- | --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `browser use`   | `browser_use`   | Committed `source`, `executablePath`, `ownership`, `version`, `compatibility`, and the `nextCommand` to run when compatibility is unverified.                                                                   |
| `browser list`  | `browser_list`  | `selection`, `effective`, `managed`, `alternatives`, `orphans`, `managedRoot`, and `driver`.                                                                                                                    |
| `browser check` | `browser_check` | `driverVersion`, `testedBuild`, `probeRevision`, the `browser` identity, and one entry per capability profile with its verdict and capability rows.                                                             |
| `doctor`        | `doctor`        | The existing check list, plus a `browser` block with the effective source, origin, ownership, executable, version, compatibility, managed root, orphan count, reclaimable bytes, alternatives, and remediation. |

Exit codes follow the established map. Invalid or conflicting flags, an unresolvable custom path, and
an unselectable managed installation are validation failures (`1`). A compatibility failure from
`browser check` and a failing doctor check are environment failures (`3`). `browser list` exits `0`
even when the selection is broken.

## Configuration and Permissions

Two keys in `config.yaml`, both reachable through `yantra config get/set/unset/validate` and both
redirected by name if you try to set them with `yantra prefs`:

| Key                       | Values                      | Default | Notes                                                                                               |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `browser.source`          | `auto`, `managed`, `system` | `auto`  | Which browser Yantra launches.                                                                      |
| `browser.executable_path` | absolute path or `null`     | `null`  | Legal only with `source: system`; rejected under the others with the repair command in the message. |

No build, version, channel, update-interval, retained-version, or Chrome-profile setting is added, and
no new environment variable is introduced. Selecting an external Chrome is not consent to use your
personal browsing data: Yantra still launches every browser with its own ephemeral, workflow, or
recording profile and still refuses real Chrome profile roots.

`browser check` writes only the local compatibility evidence cache. `browser use` writes only the two
keys above. Neither mutates a browser installation.

## Limitations

- External discovery reports the first usable Chrome or Chromium it finds, so `browser list`
  normally shows at most one external alternative rather than every browser installed on the machine.
- `browser use` proves that a path is runnable, not that it works. A binary that passes validation can
  still fail `browser check`.
- Compatibility evidence is cached per executable identity and capability profile. It is invalidated
  by a change to the executable, its version or size and timestamp, the host platform, the driver
  version, or the probe revision — but `doctor` reports what was last recorded rather than re-probing,
  so evidence is only as current as the last `browser check`.
- `browser list` and `doctor` report the orphan count and reclaimable bytes but never reclaim them.
  Collection happens during an explicit `browser install` or `browser update`.
- No command in this feature checks whether a newer browser exists. `browser list`, `browser use`,
  `browser check`, and `doctor` are local and offline; asking that question is `yantra browser update`,
  documented in [Explicit Managed Update](explicit-managed-update.md). In particular `browser check`
  probes the browser you already have and never looks for a newer one.
- The recorder takes the same selection through its core startup API; no separate recorder CLI command
  is introduced for it.
